name: PT TBS Energi Utama Tbk

frontmatter.title: TBS Energi Utama — a waste platform priced before the transition earns
frontmatter.summary: TBS is a trust-controlled energy holding mid-transition from coal to waste, renewables and electric vehicles. Waste is now most of revenue and almost all adjusted EBITDA, but the group still loses money after a full D&A charge and carries heavy segment debt. We mark the parts on their own methods: the coal reserve DCF is far below book, the waste platform above it. SELL, Rp304.
thesis: The parts are worth less than the price: a marked sum-of-the-parts less one holdco discount values the equity at Rp149, below today's Rp520.

The earlier blanket book mark was wrong in both directions: coal is worth US$40.0m on a reserve DCF against US$523.5m of segment assets, while waste is worth US$253.4m at an EV/EBITDA mark against US$492.3m of segment assets; the two corrections roughly offset in the SOTP, but not in the price.

The HPS money is preference capital at the waste subsidiary, not a distribution: at an assumed high-single to low-double-digit coupon the annual claim is US$32.6m-US$49.0m, most of the group's adjusted EBITDA, and it ranks ahead of the ordinary shares.

At the current price the shares trade at 13.2x EV/EBITDA on FY2025A restated EBITDA and about 11.8 turns on true LTM restated EBITDA of US$48.1m, above the stock's own median, and at 1.5x forecast book against an own-history mean below book.
Even our bull case, which narrows the discount, values the shares at Rp319 — below today's price; the market is pricing a waste mark above our sensitivity band.

catalysts.event: RUPSLB to approve the HPS preference investment in SBTH
NTBE floating-solar project targeted for commercial operation

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of TBS Energi Utama with a **SELL** rating and a twelve-month target of **Rp304**, a return of -41.5% from the Rp520 price. TBS is a trust-controlled energy holding that is genuinely changing shape: waste management is now the largest revenue line and the overwhelming majority of adjusted EBITDA, the coal-fired power plants are sold, and a BlackRock affiliate has agreed to put new capital into the waste platform. The transition is real. The question is what the ordinary shareholder owns after the transition is financed, and on that question the equity is expensive.

The earlier draft valued every segment at book net assets and then applied a holdco discount, which is book times a scalar rather than a valuation. This revision marks each part on its own method. The coal mines are valued on a reserve DCF at the company's own plan, net of the segment's debt proxy; the waste platform is valued at an EV/EBITDA multiple on its annualised adjusted EBITDA, net of its debt proxy; the trading, residual power and other books stay at book because there is no sourced earnings metric for them [S9, S11, S12]. The marks move in opposite directions and nearly offset: coal falls from US$523.5m of segment assets to a US$40.0m equity mark, while waste rises from US$492.3m of segment assets to US$253.4m. The marked SOTP is Rp149, the primary method at a 60% weight [S0].

The market has re-rated the stock on the HPS Investment Partners commitment of up to S$555m into SBTH, the waste holding company [S10, S15]. We do not read that commitment as value accruing to TOBA's ordinary shares on day one. HPS is buying newly issued preference shares in a subsidiary, in stages, subject to shareholder approval [S10, S15]. Preference capital ranks ahead of the ordinary equity, carries a cost, and converts a headline commitment into value for the parent only if it is deployed at returns above that cost. The announcement tells us the waste platform can attract institutional capital; it does not tell us the platform is worth the premium the market has attached to the group. The terms are not disclosed; at an assumed high-single to low-double-digit coupon the annual claim is US$32.6m-US$49.0m, most of the group's adjusted EBITDA, and the ordinary residual needs the waste segment roughly to double its EBITDA before it earns anything [S10, S12].

The cross-checks are deliberately independent and they disagree, which is the point. P/BV uses the peer median multiple on parent book equity and gives Rp309; the EV/EBITDA cross-check uses the peer median on FY2025A restated EBITDA and gives Rp737 [S0]. The marked SOTP is far below both because it deducts the segment debt and the intercompany/minority wedge that the multiples only partly capture. The blend is 60% SOTP, 30% P/BV and 10% EV/EBITDA; the earnings cross-check is weighted lightly because the peer set's EBITDA is depressed and its multiples are high, but it is included so the SELL does not rest on a book-based view alone [S0, S11, S12].

What moves the value from here: first, whether waste EBITDA keeps compounding now that it is the profit engine; second, whether the coal arm's cash cost and short reserve life hold up; third, whether the HPS money is deployed into accretive acquisitions rather than into a larger balance sheet; and fourth, whether any dated event narrows the holdco discount. On our numbers the first two are broadly priced, the third is uncertain, and the fourth has no completed catalyst. The shares trade at 1.5x our forecast book value and at 10.8x our forecast EBITDA, against a holding company that has historically traded well below forecast book [S0].

The strongest part of the bear case is also the simplest: our bull case, which assumes a ten-point narrower holdco discount, still values the shares at Rp319, below the current price [S12, S15]. To own the stock here, an investor has to believe the waste platform deserves a mark above the top of our sensitivity band, or that a large acquisition will be priced at a valuation that creates immediate parent-level value. Neither is sourced today.

TBS Energi Utama is an Indonesian energy group that began as a thermal-coal miner, listed in 2012, and renamed itself from Toba Bara Sejahtra in 2022 to mark a shift toward what it calls sustainable infrastructure [S9]. It reports in US dollars, which is unusual for an IDX coal name and matters for every ratio in this report. The group runs five reported segments: coal mining, coal trading, waste management, power generation (now a residual after the coal-fired plants were sold), and an "others" line that contains palm oil, renewable energy and electric vehicles [S8, S9].

The mix has inverted. In the first half of 2026 waste management produced 61.2% of consolidated revenue and 91.8% of adjusted EBITDA, against a coal-mining contribution of about a fifth of revenue and a small negative EBITDA [S12]. The waste platform is the group's future and, increasingly, its present. It is also the part of the group that carries the most acquired goodwill and intangible value, because it was built by acquisition rather than by organic growth.

The waste business sits under SBTH Asia Holdings Pte Ltd and operates three brands. Cora Environment is a Singapore municipal and commercial waste collector, formerly Sembcorp Environment and SembWaste, serving more than 470,000 households and businesses and operating an energy-from-waste plant with capacity of about 360,000 tonnes a year [S10, S9]. Asia Medical Enviro Services is a Singapore medical-waste specialist with about 45.0% of that market [S9]. Arah Environmental is an Indonesian medical, industrial and household waste business operating in 15.0 provinces [S9]. Collectively the three collected about 760,000 tonnes in the first half of 2026 [S15]. Cora alone collected 969,766 tonnes of municipal and commercial waste in FY2025 [S9]. The platform's economics rest on collection density, permitted facilities and long-tenured municipal contracts; the energy-from-waste plant turns non-recyclable waste into industrial steam for Jurong Island customers, which is a more stable revenue stream than merchant electricity [S10].

The coal business is smaller than the balance sheet suggests. The group holds mining concessions of about 7,087 hectares across three mine sites in East Kalimantan, operated through ABN, IM and TMU [S9]. The company estimates coal reserves of about 14 Mt with planned annual production of 3-4 Mt [S9]. In the first half of 2026 the mines produced 0.8 Mt and sold 0.6 Mt at an average selling price of US$55.2/ton, with a FOB cash cost of US$38.2/ton and a stripping ratio of 3.2x [S12]. The coal trading arm buys and sells third-party coal and is a low-margin flow business; its segment book is small [S11]. The two coal-fired power plants, with combined capacity of about two hundred megawatts, were fully divested in 2025 [S9, S17].

The smaller legs are real but sub-scale. Renewable energy consists of a 6 MW mini-hydro plant in Lampung that is operating and a 46 MWp floating-solar project in Batam that was 65.0 per cent complete at the half-year, with commercial operation targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026 [S12]. The electric-vehicle business, Electrum, had 13,883 electric two-wheelers on the road and a battery-swapping network at the half-year [S12]. Palm oil is a legacy plantation of 2,185 hectares with output of about 7,000 tonnes a year [S9]. None of these is large enough to move the group's value today, but the solar project is the clearest near-term source of incremental contracted revenue.

The group employed 1,848 people at the end of FY2025 [S9]. The controlling shareholder is Highland Strategic Holdings Pte Ltd with 60.4%; PT Toba Sejahtra holds another 8.0% [S9]. Highland is owned by a Singapore trust, GLAS Trust, acting for a passive private investment trust of institutional and high-net-worth investors; the annual report states that no single individual holds more than half of the trust [S9]. The free float is 25.7% and insiders hold 77.0% [S0]. This is a controlled company in the practical sense that matters for a minority holder: the controlling block can set strategy, approve related-party transactions and decide how much cash reaches the parent.

Indonesian holding companies owned through family or trust structures have long traded at persistent discounts to the value of the assets they control. The reasons are structural rather than cyclical: minority holders depend on cash actually being upstreamed, related-party flows run between affiliated entities, and control rarely changes hands. The market tends to price that governance reality into the multiple rather than waiting for it to resolve. A transition story can narrow the discount for a while, but the discount is the base rate, not the opportunity.

TBS straddles two industries with almost nothing in common. Thermal coal is a mature, price-taking export business. Waste management is a recurring, contract-based service business with local density advantages. The valuation has to respect both, and the group's reported mix now makes waste the dominant earnings driver even though coal still supplies most of the collateral and the balance-sheet complexity [S9, S12].

The coal industry is cyclical and the group is a small, high-cost participant in it. Indonesian thermal coal is priced off the HBA and the ICI indices, with grades and calorific values determining the discount to the benchmark. The first half of 2026 saw a sharp rally across the ICI grades, with the lower-grade ICI 4 up more than half year on year [S12]. TBS's own realised price of US$55.2/ton is well below the headline benchmarks because its coal is lower grade and its sales mix includes trading volumes [S12]. The company's cash cost of US$38.2/ton leaves a thin margin at the mine, and the group's reported coal-mining segment ran a small operating loss in the first half [S11]. The structural issue is the reserve base: about 14.0 Mt against planned production of 3-4 Mt a year is a reserve life of roughly four years [S9]. That is short enough that the coal business should be valued on a declining cash-flow profile, not on a stable multiple of current earnings.

Coal regulation matters in three ways. The royalty regime sets a floor under unit costs and is progressive with price; the domestic market obligation requires a share of output to be sold domestically at capped prices; and the environmental licensing regime governs mine expansion and closure. The group also operates in a policy environment that is pushing Indonesia away from coal-fired generation while still relying on coal for baseload power, which creates a long, noisy transition rather than a clean exit [S9]. For a small miner with a four-year reserve life, the practical effect is that the coal arm is a cash harvest, not a growth engine.

Waste management is the opposite. It is a recurring service with high local density economics, long municipal contracts and permitted facilities that are hard to replicate. Singapore's public waste collection is divided into geographic sectors, and Cora holds two of them; the energy-from-waste plant turns non-recyclable waste into industrial steam for Jurong Island [S10, S12]. The medical-waste franchise has a scale advantage and a compliance moat: AMES holds about 45.0% of the Singapore medical-waste market [S9]. In Indonesia, Arah Environmental operates across 15.0 provinces and serves medical, industrial and household customers, a market that is earlier-stage and more fragmented [S9]. The regional opportunity is real: the group argues that waste is a long value chain from collection to sorting, recycling, medical and industrial treatment, and energy recovery, and that an integrated platform can earn several revenue streams from the same tonne [S10].

Competition in waste is local and fragmented but slowly consolidating. The barriers are permits, collection density, disposal capacity and customer relationships, not capital alone. Cora's municipal contracts and its energy-from-waste plant are the closest thing TBS owns to a durable moat; the Indonesian business is more of a growth option. The risk is that the platform is built through acquisitions, and acquisition-led roll-ups can destroy value if the purchase multiples rise faster than the synergies. The HPS capital is explicitly for both organic growth and acquisitions, which is the right use of money in a consolidating market but also the point at which capital discipline matters most [S10, S15].

Renewable energy and electric vehicles are separate competitive arenas. The mini-hydro plant sells to PLN under a long-term offtake, and the floating-solar project will do the same when it reaches commercial operation [S12]. These are contracted, low-risk assets but small relative to the group. The electric-vehicle business competes in a crowded Indonesian two-wheeler and battery-swapping market with larger, better-funded players; Electrum's ecosystem and its Gojek-linked demand are advantages, but the business is sub-scale and has not yet demonstrated a durable margin [S9, S12].

A five-forces view: coal has intense rivalry, low differentiation, powerful buyers and a commodity price set externally, so returns are cyclical and the only defence is cost position and reserve quality. Waste has moderate rivalry, high barriers from permits and density, and recurring contracts, so returns are more stable and pricing power is local. Renewables have low rivalry once contracted but are policy-dependent. Electric vehicles have high rivalry and rapid technological change. Across the group, the waste business is the only one with a structural moat, and it is also the one that carries the most acquisition-related balance-sheet risk [S9, S10, S12].

External influences are mostly macro and regulatory. The group reports in US dollars but earns a large share of its waste revenue in Singapore dollars and its costs in a mix of currencies, so USD/SGD and USD/IDR matter. Coal prices drive the cash harvest. Indonesian interest rates affect the cost of the group's rupiah bonds and sukuk. Environmental policy affects both the coal exit and the waste opportunity. The macro desk's cautious stance on Indonesian rate-sensitive domestic demand is a headwind for the EV and plantation legs, while the neutral thermal-coal tilt offers no tailwind for the coal arm; its USD/IDR path of 18,350 against a spot rate of 18,025 is a headwind for rupiah-reported value, but the engine translates every method value at the spot rate of 18,025, so the forward path is context, not an input [S0]. The look-through factors that matter for a holder are thermal coal, Indonesian rates and the rupiah, Singapore waste-infrastructure demand and USD/SGD, and the EV/plantations domestic-demand beta; this is not a single-factor coal name [S9, S10, S12, S0].

The waste-management industry is being re-rated globally as investors look for infrastructure-like cash flows with environmental benefits. The attraction is that collection and treatment are essential services with recurring revenue and local barriers to entry. The risk is that the sector's growth ambitions are funded with debt and acquisitions, so the equity returns depend as much on capital allocation as on the underlying service economics. Indonesia and Singapore sit at different stages of that development, which is why a platform that spans both can look attractive on a strategic map and still be hard to value on a single multiple.

The reported history is a transition, not a steady state. Revenue fell from US$635.8m in FY2022 to US$365.9m in FY2025 as coal prices and volumes normalised and the power business moved toward divestment [S0, S8]. Gross profit fell faster, from US$136.0m to US$29.7m, because coal unit economics compressed and the acquired waste business carried a lower initial margin than the legacy coal business [S8]. The FY2025 result is not comparable with the earlier years: the group booked a loss on the divestment of the PLTU entities of about US$96.9m alongside an operating loss, and a net loss of US$161.9m [S17, S8].

The first half of 2026 shows the business after the divestments. Revenue was US$173.0m, essentially flat year on year, but gross profit more than doubled to US$28.2m as the waste mix rose and coal cash cost fell [S12, S11]. The group's adjusted EBITDA was US$25.7m, up nearly a quarter, while the net loss narrowed to US$19.4m [S12]. Operating cash flow turned positive at US$14.6m after a cash outflow in the prior-year half [S11]. The improvement is real, but it is an EBITDA improvement, not yet an earnings improvement: D&A and interest still exceed operating profit.

The revenue build is now a tale of two businesses. Waste management produced US$155.4m of the group's US$365.9m of revenue in FY2025, and the waste segment alone contributed US$51.9m in the first quarter of 2026 and the majority of first-half revenue [S3, S12]. Coal mining and trading still produced about a third of first-half revenue, and coal trading is a low-margin pass-through [S12]. Our forecast holds FY2026E revenue growth at 1.5%, close to the first-half run-rate, then accelerates to 6.0% and 5.0% as the waste build annualises and the floating solar starts producing [S12, S15]. We do not assume a large acquisition, because none is sourced; the HPS money is a financing commitment, not a completed transaction [S10, S15].

Margins are the crux of the earnings story, and the previous draft got them wrong. The FY2025 gross margin was depressed by the divestment year and weak coal prices; the first half of 2026 produced gross profit of US$28.2m on revenue of US$173.0m, a materially higher margin than FY2025 [S12, S8]. We now hold the first-half run-rate of 16.3%, fading only slightly to 16.0% long run; the earlier mark was below the last actual with no source, and there is no sourced reason for a margin squeeze in the base case. Operating expenses are the item the data pack gets wrong: the pack shows a low SG&A ratio, but the company reports selling and G&A expenses of about US$72.0m in FY2025 and US$33.2m in the first half of 2026 [S17, S12]. We model 19.2% of revenue, the first-half run-rate, not the earlier assumption [S12].

The base case is at the last actual, not below it. At the first-half run-rate the group is EBITDA-positive but still slightly EBIT-negative, because D&A is a fifth of revenue; that is the arithmetic of a capital-intensive transition, not a cautious assumption [S12]. We do not manufacture operating breakeven in the base case without a source. The path to breakeven requires roughly a two-point gross-margin expansion as waste becomes a larger share of revenue; that is a plausible bull case, and we describe it there rather than pretending it is the most likely path today [S12, S15].

The D&A restatement is the most important correction in this report, and this revision fixes it properly. The data pack's FY2025 D&A line was the general-and-administrative charge only; the audited notes show fixed-asset depreciation of US$22.2m, mine-property amortisation of US$31.3m, right-of-use depreciation of US$11.8m and intangible amortisation of US$8.8m, a full charge of US$74.1m [S8]. The engine history now carries that full charge, not the fixed-asset component alone, so FY2025 EBITDA is rebuilt at US$43.2m on the reported operating loss rather than the misleading negative figure in the earlier draft [S8, S17]. The forecast uses the post-divestment run-rate, not the FY2025 ratio: adjusted EBITDA of US$25.7m plus the operating loss of US$4.8m implies a D&A plus PLN/other add-back of US$30.5m, 17.6% of revenue [S12]. The FY2025 ratio includes divested-PLTU depreciation and higher mine amortisation and is not the forward charge [S8, S12].

Costs and cash flow tell a consistent story. FY2025 operating cash flow was US$5.2m, sharply lower than the prior year because of the divestment year and working-capital movements, while capital expenditure was US$47.1m [S8]. The first half of 2026 was better: operating cash flow of US$14.6m against fixed-asset capex of US$10.2m [S11]. The group is funding the floating-solar project and waste expansion from a combination of operating cash, the June 2026 syndicated facility and the HPS commitment [S13, S10]. Our forecast assumes capex of 10.0% of revenue, falling to 8.0% as the solar project completes, and modest net borrowing of US$15.0m in FY2026E and US$10.0m in FY2027E because the syndicated facility can fund working capital and subsidiary capex as well as refinancing [S13]. It is not purely a refinancing, so the earlier zero-borrowing assumption was too clean [S13].

The balance sheet is the constraint. At FY2025 the group had debt of US$392.9m and cash of US$85.6m, for net debt of US$307.3m; by the first half of 2026 net loans were about 5.4x adjusted EBITDA [S8, S12]. The debt sits across the coal and waste segments and is secured by subsidiary shares, receivables, inventory and project assets; the controlling shareholder's stake is not pledged, but the group's ownership interests in operating subsidiaries are pledged to lenders [S9]. The June 2026 DBS-led facility of up to S$385m refinances older loans and extends maturity, which reduces near-term refinancing risk but does not reduce leverage [S13]. A group with negative net income and net debt of this size has limited room for a value-destructive acquisition. PSAK 73 lease liabilities are small relative to the debt and are already inside finance costs, so we do not make a separate lease adjustment; the right-of-use depreciation is part of the full D&A charge [S8]. Fixed assets are carried at cost less depreciation, not under the PSAK 16 revaluation model, so the P/BV cross-check is not inflated by a revaluation reserve [S8].

Capital allocation has been active and, so far, coherent. The PLTU divestments generated about US$144.8m, which the company says was fully reallocated to waste, renewables and electric vehicles [S9]. That is the right strategic direction. The question is price discipline: the waste platform was assembled through acquisitions, and the HPS capital will fund more of them [S10, S15]. The group paid dividends of US$9.4m in FY2025 despite a net loss, which is a use of cash that a leveraged transition story can justify only if the dividend is a small share of the total [S8]. We assume a 30.0% payout once earnings recover, but the near-term DPS is zero on our negative earnings forecast. The MESOP issued shares without pre-emptive rights, taking the count from 8,249m at FY2025 toward the first-half figure; we model 0.5% a year, a small but real dilution that a minority holder should price [S8, S9, S11].

Earnings-quality flags, per the house screen. The accruals ratio is negative in each of the last three years. In FY2025 the net loss was US$161.9m against positive operating cash flow of US$5.2m, on average total assets of US$793.1m and US$893.7m; the ratio is therefore negative, not the positive accruals build that signals earnings outrunning cash [S8]. In FY2024 the group earned US$28.5m and generated US$119.1m of operating cash flow; in FY2023 earnings and cash were both positive [S8]. Cash conversion is not deteriorating in the way the Sloan ratio warns about; the FY2025 loss is driven by the disclosed divestment charge and a full D&A charge, both non-cash [S8, S17]. Receivables are not growing faster than revenue: the FY2025 receivables balance is modest relative to sales, and inventory fell as coal volumes fell [S8]. The real flags are structural rather than accounting: the group's reported profit is negative after a full D&A charge, the minority interest and preference claims sit ahead of the parent's ordinary equity at the waste subsidiary, and related-party balances are concentrated around the controlling shareholder [S8]. We classify the related-party receivable as an optics-class flag, not a manipulation-class one: it was disclosed, interest-bearing and transferred at the same tenor, but its reclassification to a third party whose ownership is not disclosed weakens transparency [S8]. There is no evidence of fabricated cash or fictitious revenue. The item we cannot close is the recoverability of the coal segment's book value against a reserve life of roughly four years; that is a valuation question, and we treat it in the valuation section [S9, S11].

The company's adjusted EBITDA needs a reconciliation, not just a label. The definition is operating income plus D&A plus PLN billed receivables plus others [S12]. For FY2025, adjusted EBITDA of US$47.2m less the reported operating loss of US$-31.0m and the full D&A charge of US$74.1m leaves only a small single-digit million non-D&A residual; almost all of the add-back is D&A and only a thin tail is the "PLN billed receivables plus others" bucket [S12, S8]. At the segment level the first half of 2026 shows the same pattern: waste adjusted EBITDA of US$47.2m on an annualised basis sits against waste operating profit of US$1.4m, so the gap is large and must be mostly D&A [S12, S11]. The segment D&A split is not disclosed, so we cannot attribute the gap line by line; the group-level evidence that the add-back is overwhelmingly D&A is what makes the adjusted measure a reasonable operating proxy rather than a hidden "other" [S12, S8]. We classify the residual as optics-class: disclosed, but not fully itemised [S12].

The house card for holding companies and conglomerates calls for a sum of the parts with honest marks, less holdco net debt, less a holdco discount, with the discount treated as the base rate rather than the opportunity [S0]. TBS fits that method better than a consolidated multiple, because the group contains a declining coal miner, a low-margin trading business, a residual power book, a growing waste platform and a set of small optionality assets. A single EV/EBITDA multiple would price the consolidated leverage and the mix together and would tell us very little about what the ordinary shareholder owns after the subsidiary claims.

Our cost of equity builds from a risk-free rate of 5.0%, an equity risk premium of 4.2% plus a country premium of 2.5%, and an unlevered beta of 0.9 levered to 2.1 at the group's debt-to-equity ratio [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 18.8% and a WACC of 10.5%. The high levered beta is doing most of the work: the group's consolidated debt is large relative to its equity, and the cost of debt of 7.0% is the market rate on its rupiah and dollar facilities [S13].

The primary method is a segment sum of the parts with per-segment marks, less the consolidation elimination and minority claims, less a 30.0% holdco discount. The coal mark is a reserve DCF, not book: 14 Mt of reserves at the company's 3-4 Mt/yr plan, a US$55.2/ton selling price and US$38.2/ton cash cost give a thin per-tonne margin; after sustaining capex, tax at the statutory rate, the rehabilitation provision of US$11.0m and a 10.5% discount, the enterprise value is roughly US$131.2m of debt plus the equity mark, and after the segment's debt proxy the equity is US$40.0m [S9, S11, S12]. At the actual annualised production rate the DCF does not cover the debt and the equity value is negative; we use the plan-based mark because the company's plan is the most likely volume path under the house method, and it is the more generous of the two [S12, F42]. The coal segment's FY2025 operating loss of US$29.8m and its 14 Mt reserve base do not support the US$523.5m of segment assets carried at book [S8, S9, S11]. Tax is the one assumption that flatters this mark: the DCF uses the statutory twenty-two per cent rate, while the last paid effective rate was just under thirty-eight per cent on FY2024 [S8]; at that rate the coal mark would fall by roughly three-quarters and the blended target by about twenty-seven rupiah. That is an optimistic tilt in a SELL case, so we disclose it rather than book it [S8].

The waste mark is an EV/EBITDA mark, not book: annualised first-half adjusted EBITDA of US$47.2m at the stock's own-history EV/EBITDA median - the median of its datapack observations, which is ten point eight turns rather than the round ten used in the earlier draft - gives US$253.4m of equity after deducting the US$255.9m segment debt proxy, a little over three times the segment's book net assets [S0, S12, S11]. The multiple is the sourced median, not a discount to it; the low-to-high band around it is an analyst sensitivity range rather than a house one, and at its ends the mark is US$74.5m and US$310.5m [S0, S12]. The 16 October inbreng values the SBT operating company at S$138.2m, which is a related-party subscription price rather than an arm's-length common-equity mark and sits well below our base mark [S16]. The segment's 1H 2026 operating profit of US$1.4m is small against its US$47.2m annualised adjusted EBITDA, which is exactly why we value the platform on EBITDA and disclose the D&A gap rather than pretending the operating profit is the earnings base [S11, S12]. The trading, residual power and others books stay at book net assets of US$26.1m less US$13.7m, US$82.1m less US$4.3m, and US$94.3m less US$50.7m; there is no sourced segment earnings metric for a flow business, a residual power book and a set of development assets, and the development assets are carried at least at sunk capex [S11, S12].

The marks move in opposite directions and largely offset in the SOTP. Coal falls from US$523.5m of segment assets to a US$40.0m equity mark; waste rises from US$492.3m of segment assets to US$253.4m. The gross parts fall from the earlier book sum to Rp149 after the holdco net-debt wedge and the discount. That is the honest answer to the earlier FATAL: the blanket book mark was not a valuation, but the corrected marks do not produce a different order of magnitude for the SOTP; they produce a different distribution, with the coal overstatement and the waste understatement roughly cancelling [S9, S11, S12].

The discount is applied once, to marked value, and it is anchored rather than asserted. The 30.0% sits in the middle of the persistent band the card uses for family- or trust-controlled Indonesian holdcos, and there is no dated, completed discount-narrowing catalyst: the HPS preference is a financing, not a cash distribution, and it still needs RUPSLB approval [S9, S15]. The stock's own P/BV history has traded both below and above book, with FY2025A the high observation; we use the peer median of 0.85 for the cross-check rather than the own-history mean because the peer set is the consistent comparator at the valuation date [S0]. The relevant premium is the one the price pays over the parts: Rp520 against a pre-discount SOTP of Rp149 divided by the complement of the discount. The price is a premium, not a discount, and the report should say so plainly [S0].

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is informative. P/BV at the peer median multiple of 0.85 times parent book gives Rp309, which is 107.2% above the marked SOTP [S0]. The gap exists because the SOTP deducts the segment debt and the intercompany/minority wedge while P/BV capitalises the parent's reported equity directly; P/BV is the more generous of the two and still sits well below the current price. The EV/EBITDA cross-check at the peer median of 15.54 times FY2025A restated EBITDA gives Rp737, above both the SOTP and P/BV; it is the one cross-check that says the shares are cheap, and we weight it at 10% only because the peer set's EBITDA is depressed and its multiples are high [S0, S12]. The metric is labelled on the last audited fiscal year, not true LTM: on true LTM restated EBITDA of US$48.1m (FY2025A restated less the prior-year half plus the current half) the price is about 11.8 turns and the cross-check value would be about twenty rupiah per share higher on the 10% weight, so the target is, if anything, a touch below a true-LTM basis, not above it [S12, F114, F115]. The own-history EV/EBITDA observations are a median of about ten and eight-tenths turns, which is the multiple we apply to the waste platform, and a mean distorted by a year of depressed EBITDA; at the median the equity is worth materially less than the peer-median result, close to our target [S0]. A P/E cross-check is unavailable because last-twelve-month parent earnings are negative [S8]. The valuation table shows all three methods and their weights.

The market's own multiple is the cleanest way to see the gap. At the current price the shares trade at 1.5x our forecast book value and 10.8x our forecast EBITDA, but the more relevant numbers are the trailing ones: 1.2x trailing book and 13.2x on restated FY2025A EBITDA, which is about 11.8 turns on a true-LTM basis [S0, F115]. The book multiple is the one that matters for a holdco: the stock's own five-year mean is 0.85 times book and FY2025A was the high observation; the current price is a premium to that history [S0]. The EV/EBITDA multiple looks less demanding on the forward forecast, but it is measured on a consolidated EBITDA that includes the coal cash harvest and sits on top of debt that is secured against the operating assets; it is not a clean measure of the equity's earning power.

The sensitivity table shows the range around the target. The maximum cell is at the ten-point narrower holdco discount and one-point lower cost of equity, and the minimum cell is at the ten-point wider discount and one-point higher cost of equity; both corners are close to, but slightly inside, the bull and bear scenario values because the scenarios carry the discount shock while the grid holds the other inputs at base [S12]. The grid central cell is the target. The current price is above the top of that range. We no longer claim the reverse DCF "does not bracket" the price as if it had solved for a discount: the solver searches the holdco discount and returns unavailable because the primary SOTP value at the widest premium in its search range is still below the price; the price is therefore a premium to the marked NAV, not a discount to it [S0, S12].

The HPS transaction deserves a separate word because it is the apparent justification for the re-rating. HPS is committing up to S$555m of new preference capital to SBTH in stages, subject to a shareholder vote [S10, S15]. Preference shares are a claim on the subsidiary ahead of the ordinary equity. At inception, a fair-value preference investment adds cash and an equal claim, so it does not create parent-level value by itself; it creates value only through what the cash earns. The bridge therefore carries the cash and the matching claim at the same probability, and they net to zero [S10, S15]. If the money funds acquisitions at returns above the preference cost, the ordinary equity benefits from the spread. If it funds acquisitions at high prices, the preference claim absorbs the first returns and the ordinary equity bears the downside. The coupon is not disclosed; at an assumed high-single to low-double-digit rate the annual claim is US$32.6m to US$49.0m, most of the group's adjusted EBITDA, and the ordinary residual needs the waste segment roughly to double its EBITDA before it earns anything [S10, S12, F101, F102]. At a ten, twenty, thirty or fifty per cent conversion stake the implied SBTH common-equity value is US$3,672.8m, US$1,632.4m, US$952.2m or US$408.1m respectively, far above the inbreng marker; those are not credible common-equity marks, which is why we treat the preference as debt-like mezzanine rather than as a value marker [S10, S16]. We therefore do not add the HPS headline to the valuation bridge as a net positive; we add it gross and subtract the matching claim, and we quantify the coupon as a claim on the waste cash flow [S10, S15].

The rating thresholds are explicit. Holding the other segments and the cross-checks fixed, the SELL band is left - the return reaches the minus twenty-five per cent REDUCE boundary - at a waste mark of about US$332.6m (roughly twelve and a half turns of annualised EBITDA); REDUCE runs from there to about US$404.6m (about fourteen turns), where the return reaches the minus ten per cent HOLD threshold; price parity is reached only at US$452.6m, roughly fifteen turns and six times the segment's book, above the top of our sensitivity band [S12]. On the earlier framework that held coal at book, price parity needed only a low-single-digit multiple of waste book; the coal mark-down removes roughly a quarter of a billion dollars of value, so the waste hurdle rises. The SELL survives the full low-to-high band and survives a premium conversion of the preference unless HPS's stake is small and the platform is re-marked above the top of our band [S10, S12].

The bull and bear cases are honest about the range. The bull case assumes the HPS capital is deployed well, waste EBITDA compounds, coal cash cost stays low and the discount narrows; it values the shares at Rp319. The bear case assumes coal weakness, slow deployment, a preference coupon that absorbs waste cash and a wider discount; it values the shares at Rp289 [S12, S15]. The base case at Rp304 sits between them, and the current price sits above both. That is the core of the call: this is not a valuation that requires a pessimistic view of the transition. It requires only that the transition be financed on terms that leave something for the ordinary shareholder, which the current price does not.

The downside risks are real and they are not all in the bear case. **Regulatory risk** is medium-likelihood and high-impact: the coal royalty schedule, the domestic market obligation and the environmental licensing regime can change the coal arm's unit economics, and the waste franchise depends on municipal contracts and permitted facilities in two jurisdictions [S9, S10]. **Commodity risk** is high-likelihood and medium-impact: TBS is a price-taker in thermal coal, its realised price is well below the headline benchmarks, and a weaker ICI complex would compress the cash harvest before the waste platform is large enough to offset it [S12, S9]. **Execution risk** is medium-likelihood and high-impact: the waste platform is acquisition-led, the HPS money is staged, and the floating-solar project has to reach commercial operation on schedule to deliver the contracted revenue [S12, S10].

**Governance risk** is medium-likelihood and high-impact. Insiders hold 77.0% of the shares, with the controlling shareholder at 60.4%, the group is owned through a Singapore trust, and the waste platform's capital structure now includes a preference claim that ranks ahead of the ordinary equity [S9, S10]. Related-party transactions are small in absolute terms, but the inbreng of SBT shares through SBTI, SBTH and SBTG was completed as an intra-group restructuring without a fairness opinion because the entities are almost wholly owned [S16]. That is legally clean, but it shows how easily value can be moved between affiliated entities without a market test. **Liquidity risk** is low-likelihood and medium-impact: the free float is 25.7%, the stock trades with reasonable liquidity, and the group has refinanced its near-term bank debt, but a leveraged holding company with a thin float can gap on news [S0, S13].

**Currency and rate risk** is medium-likelihood and medium-impact. The group reports in US dollars, earns Singapore dollars in the waste business, and carries rupiah bonds and sukuk; a stronger dollar or higher Indonesian rates raise the cost of the rupiah debt and compress the translated value of the domestic businesses [S8, S13]. **Operational risk** in waste is medium-likelihood and medium-impact: collection density, plant availability and integration of acquired businesses determine whether the segment's EBITDA converts into cash [S12]. **Coal reserve risk** is the quiet one: with about 14.0 Mt of reserves against planned production of 3-4 Mt a year, the coal arm has a short life, and a failure to replace reserves would turn the cash harvest into a run-off [S9].

The scenarios mirror the same driver: the holdco discount. The bear case widens it by ten points and the bull case narrows it by ten points, with probabilities of 25.0%, 50.0% and 25.0% [S12, S15]. The bear value is Rp289, the base is Rp304 and the bull is Rp319. The scenario table tests the discount only, and we say so plainly: the SOTP marks are struck at dated values and the consolidated forecast does not re-price them, so neither a revenue-growth shock nor a waste re-mark can be wired into it. The driver-based range the reader should use is therefore given directly on the waste multiple: at the low end of the band the blended target is Rp198, at the own-history median it is the base Rp304 and at the high end Rp366, so a 25.0%/50.0%/25.0% weighting across that band gives about Rp293 - still a SELL at every corner, the high end returning about minus thirty per cent. Those driver marks move the target far more than the discount, and the price sits above the top of that band [S12, S0].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A segment-level disclosure that lets us mark the waste platform on its own cash flows rather than its book net assets would be the most important. A completed, priced acquisition that shows the HPS money being deployed at a valuation accretive to the parent would be the second. A coal reserve upgrade or a long-term offtake that extends the mine life would be the third. A dated, completed discount-narrowing event — a buyback, a tender, a structural dividend increase from the waste subsidiary — would be the fourth. On the other side, a preference term sheet that gives HPS a conversion or upside participation at the expense of the ordinary equity would widen the discount, not narrow it [S10, S15].

Control is concentrated and the structure is opaque at the top. Highland Strategic Holdings holds 60.4% and PT Toba Sejahtra holds 8.0%; Highland is owned by GLAS Trust, a Singapore trust acting for a passive private investment trust, and the annual report says no single individual holds more than half of the trust [S9]. The free float is 25.7% and insiders hold 77.0% [S0]. The practical consequence is that minority shareholders have little influence over strategy, related-party transactions or the pace of the transition. The board includes independent commissioners with relevant backgrounds, and the annual report discloses no material administrative sanctions against the company or its directors and commissioners in FY2025 [S9]. We found no special-monitoring-board notation or adverse notation letter in the filings reviewed; the free float is above the exchange's minimum and the shares remain in the ordinary board [S9, S0].

The auditor is KAP Purwantono, Sungkoro & Surja, a member of the EY network, and it issued an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 consolidated financial statements [S9]. The audit was signed by Benyanto Suherman, and the financial statements were signed by the board on 9 March 2026 [S9]. An unqualified opinion from a tier-one firm is a baseline comfort, not a substitute for reading the notes; the D&A restatement in this report comes from exactly those notes [S8].

Related-party dealings are small in the reported numbers but structurally important, and this revision quantifies them. At FY2024 the group carried a non-current other receivable from its controlling shareholder Highland of US$37.7m, a meaningful share of parent equity and total assets, under a 2017 Acknowledgement of Indebtedness that was extended in December 2024 to eighteen years at a raised rate and then assigned on 30 June 2025 to CDG Trading Limited at the same maturity and a further-raised rate of 680.0% [S8, F88, F91]. The assignment did not take a loss: the FY2025 non-current third-party other receivables line rises to US$43.2m from a much smaller base, which is where the balance now sits [S8]. Interest income from Highland was US$0.7m in FY2025, a fifth of finance income, so the receivable is not a dead balance [S8]. CDG Trading's ownership and its relationship to the controller are not disclosed in the FY2025 notes; the assignment was signed by the company, Highland and CDG, but the group does not classify CDG as a related party after the transfer [S8]. We classify this as an optics-class flag: the balance was disclosed and interest-bearing, but a related-party receivable reclassified to an undisclosed third party weakens transparency and is exactly the channel through which value can move between affiliated entities [S8]. Related-party flows are not material as a share of revenue; the interest income is the main recurring item [S8].

The inbreng needs the same scrutiny. On 16 October 2026 the group moved its SBT shares through SBTI, SBTH and SBTG at a stated S$138.2m, with each entity issuing new shares at an agreed subscription price; no fairness opinion was required because the entities are almost wholly owned [S16]. The basis is an intra-group subscription price, not an independent appraisal, so we treat it as a weak marker for the SBT operating company rather than as fair value for the whole waste segment [S16]. The sequencing matters: the waste opco was moved under SBTH immediately before HPS takes newly issued preference shares in SBTH, which is the entity where HPS will rank ahead of the parent's ordinary equity [S10, S16]. The transfer itself does not shift value between shareholders because the entities were already almost wholly owned, but it concentrates the waste assets under the preference-bearing entity, so HPS's claim attaches to the whole platform rather than to a slice; that is a value-transfer channel in the direction of the preference holder, and a minority holder should price it [S10, S16].

On pledges, the company's shares in operating subsidiaries are pledged to lenders under the ADB, TLB and SEF facilities, and the group's bank accounts, receivables and inventories are also collateral [S9]. The controlling shareholder's shares in TOBA are not disclosed as pledged in the annual report. That distinction matters: a pledge of subsidiary shares is normal project finance, while a pledge of the controlling block would be a margin-call supply risk. We found no evidence of the latter in the sources reviewed [S9].

The dividend record is mixed. The group paid cash dividends of US$17.5m in FY2025, including the minority share, despite a net loss, and the trailing DPS is Rp18.6 [S8, S0]. A dividend through a loss year is a signal that the controlling shareholder values cash distributions, but it is also a use of cash that a leveraged transition story can justify only if the payout is small relative to the group's funding needs. We assume the dividend is suspended on our negative near-term earnings forecast and resumes at a modest payout once earnings recover [S8].

ESG is central to this equity rather than incidental. The group's stated strategy is a decarbonisation transition, and the PLTU divestments cut carbon emissions by about 80.0% [S9]. The waste platform is the ESG asset: collection, recycling, medical-waste treatment and energy-from-waste are all part of the environmental-services economy [S10]. The social dimension is also real: Cora serves hundreds of thousands of households and businesses, and Arah serves medical and industrial customers across many provinces [S10, S9]. The governance dimension is the weak link: a trust-controlled holding company with a preference-share financing at a subsidiary and a history of intra-group restructurings has to earn its discount, not assume it away [S9, S16].

Indonesian listed companies with concentrated ownership are increasingly judged on free float, related-party discipline and the treatment of minority holders. The market's tolerance for opaque holding structures has fallen as index providers and regulators have tightened their scrutiny. A company that can demonstrate a clean audit, a credible board and a clear capital-allocation policy can narrow the governance discount over time; one that cannot should expect the discount to persist. The transition story does not change that arithmetic; it only changes the size of the assets the discount is applied to.

The nearest dated catalysts are the shareholder meeting to approve the HPS preference investment and the floating-solar commercial operation date [S15, S12]. The HPS transaction is the more important of the two: the terms of the preference shares, the staging schedule and the first acquisition will tell us whether the waste platform's capital is being raised on terms that leave value for the ordinary shareholder [S10, S15]. The floating-solar project is smaller but cleaner: it is a contracted asset, it is already substantially complete, and commercial operation would add a visible revenue line to the renewable segment [S12].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are: waste revenue and adjusted EBITDA share, Cora's collected tonnage and plant availability, the coal cash cost and stripping ratio, the coal reserve statement, net debt to adjusted EBITDA, the holdco discount to our SOTP, and the HPS deployment schedule [S12, S9, S10]. We also watch the related-party disclosures and any change in the preference terms, because those are the channels through which the value of the waste platform reaches — or does not reach — the parent's ordinary shareholders [S8, S16].

The monitoring plan is deliberately simple. If waste EBITDA compounds and the HPS money is deployed at accretive prices, the SOTP rises and the discount can narrow; if the coal cash harvest holds, the group can fund the transition without new parent debt; if the discount narrows on a completed event, the target moves up [S12, S10]. None of those has happened yet. Until they do, the balance of evidence supports a SELL at the current price [S10, S15].
